title: Redwood: concise positioning and go-to-market hooks
content:
Purpose: a compact one-pager to align marketing, sales, and product on the core ‘why Redwood’ narrative. This is intentionally pragmatic — focused on the buying triggers we see in mid-market SaaS and platform teams building LLM features.

One-line (elevator):
Redwood makes inference predictable, fast, and cost-effective across hosted, reserved, and private deployments — so engineering teams ship LLM features without building or babysitting an inference stack.

Core thesis:
As models become commoditized, the customer value shifts to how you serve them: latency, cost per inference, uptime under real traffic, and operational controls. Teams win not by owning models but by owning reliable, efficient inference. Redwood is the unified runtime and control plane that turns inference into a predictable product for engineers and platform teams.

Three messaging pillars (customer-facing):
- Operational predictability: SLA-backed performance and predictable spend so product teams can plan capacity and SLAs.
- Deployment flexibility: same API and tooling across hosted, dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and private (VPC/on-prem) so customers don’t refactor as requirements evolve.
- Cost-conscious performance: runtime, batching, caching, and quantization recommendations that materially lower per-token cost while preserving quality.

Proof points / features to call out:
- Unified REST/SDK interface for text, chat, embeddings, and reranking (single integration across deployment modes).
- Dedicated capacity with burst and autoscale options for predictable throughput.
- Private control plane and KMS/HSM integrations for regulated workloads.
- Console observability: token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks, per-model dashboards, and rollout controls (canary, A/B, automatic fallback).
- Optimize tooling: automatic batching/caching suggestions and model quantization recommendations tied to workload patterns.

Target buyer personas and triggers:
- Platform/Infra lead at a growth SaaS (10–200 engs): needs predictable latency for chat or document search, worried about token costs and burst behavior. Trigger: an experiment that doubled inference spend.
- ML infra lead at enterprise product team: requires private deployment + KMS and audit logs. Trigger: procurement/security review.
- CTO/Head of Engineering at AI-native startup: wants fast time-to-market and predictable cost for PLG feature. Trigger: first paid customers causing scaling pain.

Primary objections and concise rebuttals: 
- “We can host models ourselves.” — Rebuttal: building high-throughput inference, KV cache management, autoscaling, and observability is a full-time operational burden; Redwood abstracts that with verified perf and predictable economics so your team can focus on product.
- “Vendor lock-in risk.” — Rebuttal: Single API across hosted/dedicated/private and model versioning means customers can move between modes without rewriting call surfaces; routing policies and fallback keep apps resilient.
- “Price concerns vs raw cloud GPU.” — Rebuttal: Redwood’s batching, caching, and model variants reduce per-token cost and operational overhead; for many workloads total TCO is lower than DIY.

Competitive angle (high-level battlecards):
- Cloud AI platforms (big clouds): Strength: broad infra + billing consolidation. Weakness: generic endpoints, less inference-specific optimizations, and slower iteration on LLM serving features. Hook: emphasize inference-first runtime and cost controls that cloud endpoints don’t provide today.
- LLM API providers (simplicity-first): Strength: extremely easy to call. Weakness: limited deployment modes, less control for regulated customers or heavy workloads. Hook: show path from quick API to enterprise-ready dedicated/private without rewrites.
- Self-hosted runtimes / OSS stacks: Strength: control and cost potential. Weakness: operational complexity and slower time to production. Hook: offer a migration template (audit + runbook) and numbers showing engineering hours saved and latency improvements.

Sample headlines and subheads for collateral:
- Headline: "Inference that behaves like infrastructure"
  Subhead: "Predictable performance, lower unit cost, and a single API from prototype to private deployment."
- Headline: "Turn inference into a predictable engineering deliverable"
  Subhead: "SLA-backed capacity, tooling for cost and quality, and private deployment options for regulated teams."

Sales hooks / talk tracks:
- For platform teams: "We’ll show you per-token cost and a plan to cut unit spend 30% in 30 days by enabling caching and better batching — with no app changes."
- For security/compliance: "We run a private control plane and support KMS/HSM + audit logs — you get vendor-grade observability without giving up network controls."
- For startups: "Start on hosted API; when you need predictability we map you to dedicated capacity with identical API and an agreed rollout plan."

Open questions (for product/marketing alignment):
- Can we publish three concrete workload case studies (chat, embeddings at scale, reranking) with before/after cost & latency numbers?
- Which unique benchmarks can we run vs top cloud AI endpoints to clearly quantify latency or cost delta?
- What is the minimum set of security artifacts (SOC2 summary, encryption at rest notes, private deployment runbook) we can publish for sales enablement?

Next steps (short list):
- Product: confirm we can share anonymized workload numbers for 3 customers (owner: Priya).
- Analytics: produce a simple benchmark doc comparing latency and cost vs two public endpoints for 512-token chat (owner: Olu).
- GTM: draft a 1-pager battlecard for each competitor category with objection scripts and proof points (owner: Leah).

Notes to self / informal:
- Keep language focused on engineering value (not generic “AI acceleration”). Engineers and platform buyers care about predictability and invoices.
- Avoid technical deep dives in the front page — use appendices.
- This should be the canonical short narrative we push into sales play, website hero copy tests, and new-entrant email outreach.

Document history: initial draft 2025-02-10 by Marcus; quick revisions after feedback session 2025-02-12.
